title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
1. The quality manager’s brief

Harnswell manufactures precision cam rollers for sewing machines.
Oversized parts may be downgraded; undersized parts may become scrap.
Source: Basic Business Statistics, ninth edition, Chapter 18, pp. 752–754.
Unit: one roller diameter, in inches; five measurements per production batch for 30 batches.
Engineering limits: 0.5072 to 0.5075 inches, inclusive.
Period: source batch order is retained; calendar dates are not supplied in the CSV.
The workbook column Day is represented here as batch, consistent with the case’s production subgroups.
Limit: the historical case narrative does not establish that temperature alone caused the observed variation.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
4. A short process-control primer

Within-batch variation concerns the five rollers in one subgroup.
Between-batch changes may indicate shifts in centering or operating conditions.
An R chart tracks within-batch ranges; an X-bar chart tracks batch means.
Check the R chart first: unstable within-batch variation undermines interpretation of X-bar limits.
Control limits estimate expected variation for a stable process; specification limits describe acceptable products.
A stable process can still produce unacceptable parts.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
5. Estimate initial chart limits

For subgroup size five, use A2 = 0.577, D3 = 0, D4 = 2.114.
X-bar limits: grand mean ± A2 × average range.
R limits: D3 × average range and D4 × average range.
These are initial Phase I limits estimated using all 30 batches, including any unusual batches.


subgroups <- rollers %>% group_by(batch) %>%
  summarise(xbar = mean(diameter), R = max(diameter) - min(diameter),
    n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>% arrange(batch)
stopifnot(all(subgroups$n == 5))
xbarbar <- mean(subgroups$xbar)
Rbar <- mean(subgroups$R)
xlimits <- xbarbar + c(-1, 1) * .577 * Rbar
rlimits <- c(0, 2.114 * Rbar)
knitr::kable(data.frame(chart = c("X-bar", "R"),
  centre = c(xbarbar, Rbar), lower = c(xlimits[1], rlimits[1]),
  upper = c(xlimits[2], rlimits[2])), digits = 7)

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
section: 7. Capability requires a stable, suitable process model
text:
7. Capability requires a stable, suitable process model

Cp compares specification width with six within-process standard deviations.
Cpk also accounts for the process mean’s distance from each specification limit.
With subgroup size five, an estimate of within-process SD is average range / d2, where d2 = 2.326.
The initial charts signal instability, so a reliable capability claim is not supported by this initial dataset.
The following template is intentionally not executed. Use it only after a documented stability investigation and suitable distribution/measurement checks.


# stable_subgroups must come from a justified, documented process phase.
mu <- mean(stable_subgroups$xbar)
sigma_within <- mean(stable_subgroups$R) / 2.326
Cp <- (USL - LSL) / (6 * sigma_within)
Cpk <- min((USL - mu) / (3 * sigma_within),
           (mu - LSL) / (3 * sigma_within))


A negative Cpk indicates a fitted mean beyond a specification limit; it is not a negative defect percentage.
Do not convert Cp or Cpk into a guaranteed future defect rate without the additional model assumptions.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
8. Independent quality-improvement briefing

Reproduce specification counts and percentages from the 150 measurements.
Report the initial R and X-bar limits with units and appropriate decimal precision.
Explain how batch 17 can signal a shift even though none of its individual measurements is below specification.
Propose records to examine: temperature, warm-up, setup, tooling and measurement calibration.
The book describes a cold-start explanation and corrective action. Explain why the narrative is insufficient to prove causality in the CSV alone.
As a retrospective sensitivity analysis, recalculate limits excluding batch 17, retain the original results and state what evidence would justify treating it as a separate process condition.
Explain why recalculated limits alone do not validate future process stability or capability.
Recommend how to collect new subgroups after an intervention, and distinguish reducing variation from shifting the process mean.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
Submission

Specification table, both initial control charts and the flagged-batch table.
A 150–200-word improvement memo addressing stability, compliance, the source discrepancy and next measurements.
Include a justified comparison of original and sensitivity results if assigned; keep capability claims conditional.

Perfect Parachute purchases synthetic fibre from four suppliers.
Five parachutes per supplier are woven and tested to breaking point.
Source: Basic Business Statistics, ninth edition, Chapter 11, pp. 388 and 393–399.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
text:
3. A short ANOVA introduction

Separate variation between supplier means from variation within suppliers.
ANOVA divides each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom to form a mean square.
F = between-group mean square / within-group mean square.
A large F is evidence against equal population means under the model.
Null: all four population mean strengths are equal.
Alternative: at least one differs; the test does not say that all pairs differ.
Classical one-way ANOVA assumes independent errors, approximately normal errors within groups and a common error variance.


fit <- aov(strength ~ supplier, data = parachutes)
summary(fit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
supplier     3  63.29  21.095   3.462 0.0414 *
Residuals   16  97.50   6.094                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



aov() fits the one-factor model; supplier is categorical, not a numeric trend.
F is approximately 3.462, with p approximately 0.0414.
At 5%, the model gives evidence against all four means being equal.

Read each contrast’s direction and interval; do not rank suppliers using p-values alone.
An overall significant test need not make every pair significant.
These intervals concern mean differences, not minimum guaranteed product strength.

plot(fit, which = 1)
plot(fit, which = 2)







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
fligner.test(strength ~ supplier, data = parachutes)


    Fligner-Killeen test of homogeneity of variances

data:  strength by supplier
Fligner-Killeen:med chi-squared = 0.55853, df = 3, p-value = 0.9059



Residual plots assess spread and approximate normality; they cannot establish independent assignment.
fligner.test() checks dispersion; a large p-value does not prove equal variances.
Five observations per supplier give imprecise diagnostics.
Causal supplier claims need a defensible assignment protocol and control of weaving/testing conditions.


Optional: relax the equal-variance assumption

oneway.test(strength ~ supplier, data = parachutes, var.equal = FALSE)


    One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances)

data:  strength and supplier
F = 3.3206, num df = 3.0000, denom df = 8.7743, p-value = 0.07206



Welch’s one-way test avoids assuming equal variances.
Tukey intervals from the classical model do not automatically become Welch-compatible pairwise intervals.
Report sensitivity openly rather than choosing the method giving the preferred answer.

text:

Explain F using the observed between- and within-supplier variation.
Identify the largest sample mean difference and report its Tukey interval and adjusted p-value.
Compare classical and Welch conclusions, including their assumptions.
Explain why five tests per supplier cannot establish rare failure rates or minimum guaranteed strength.
Specify additional evidence on cost, delivery reliability and engineering requirements before recommending a supplier.
Propose a follow-up experiment controlling loom conditions and assigning fibre treatments appropriately.

title: Extended Case 2 — Oxford Cereal

4. See the sampling distribution

This simulation generates hypothetical normal-process weights under a 368 g mean and 15 g SD.
Its values are not observed Oxford measurements.


set.seed(42001)
sim_means <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(n, mean = mu0, sd = sigma)))
ggplot(data.frame(sample_mean = sim_means), aes(sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = petra_accent, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = xbar, colour = petra_ink, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean of 25 simulated boxes (g)", y = "Simulated samples")









set.seed() makes the simulation reproducible.
replicate() repeats the hypothetical sampling experiment.
The vertical line marks the reported sample mean, 372.5 g.

title: Extended Case 2 — Oxford Cereal
text:
5. Test the process mean

Null: the population mean is 368 g.
Alternative: the population mean differs from 368 g.
Decision threshold: 5%, two-sided.


z <- (xbar - mu0) / se
p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
ci <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) * se
knitr::kable(data.frame(z = z, p_value = p_value,
  lower_mean_g = ci[1], upper_mean_g = ci[2], reject = p_value < alpha), digits = 4)

pnorm() gives the normal tail probability; the two tails account for deviations in either direction.
The result is Z = 1.50, with p about 0.134.

title: Practical 3 — Superstore discounts and profit
text:
1. The commercial manager’s question

Which product groups deserve a discount and profitability review?


Source: Tableau’s fictitious Superstore, downloaded 6 November 2026.
Scope: US orders placed in 2023–2025.
Line analysis: 6,682 product lines for categories and discount bands.
Order analysis: 3,322 orders for basket sales and profit.
Units: sales and profit in dollars; discount as a fraction.
Limit: discount decisions were not randomized; product mix and other factors differ across groups.

title: Practical 3 — Superstore discounts and profit

source("lessons/_includes/course-tools.R")
lines <- read.csv("data/business/superstore-lines.csv",
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(postal_code = "character"))
orders <- make_orders(lines)
lines <- lines %>% mutate(
  line_margin_pct = 100 * profit / sales,
  loss_line = profit < 0,
  discount_band = cut(discount, breaks = c(-Inf, 0, .2, Inf),
    labels = c("None", "Above 0 to 20%", "Above 20%"), ordered_result = TRUE))
stopifnot(!anyNA(lines$discount_band), all(lines$sales > 0))

A line’s margin is profit divided by its recorded sales.

title: 3.1 Probability Distributions
text:
What does statistical inference do?
Statistical inference uses sample data to draw conclusions about a population and quantify the uncertainty in those conclusions. It helps us estimate unknown features, test claims and assess relationships.



Original probability slides, source slide 3. Sampling moves from population to sample; inference reasons back to the population.



Population: the group or process we want to understand.
Sample: the observations we actually collect.
Parameter: a population feature, such as mean product strength, μ\mu.
Statistic: a sample calculation, such as sample mean strength, x‾\bar x.








Question
What inference contributes




What is the mean product strength?
An estimate and an uncertainty interval.


Does a store display change sales?
Evidence from a comparison designed to answer that question.


How does price relate to sales?
An estimated relationship, with assumptions and limits.



How the data are obtained affects the conclusion

Random sampling helps a sample represent a defined population.
Random assignment helps isolate a treatment comparison in an experiment.

Sampling supports conclusions about a population; assignment supports a causal comparison. Neither is established merely by calculating a probability.

title: 3.1 Probability Distributions
section: Binomial: defective cars in a batch
text:
Binomial: defective cars in a batch
A binomial distribution describes the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same success probability. Here, “success” means a car is classified as defective; it does not mean a desirable outcome.
Question: how many of 80 cars might be defective if the defect probability is 2%?
Let X=X= number of defective cars among the 80 cars.
X∼Binomial⁡(n=80,p=0.02).X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n=80,p=0.02).
The binomial model assumes:

A fixed number of trials: 80 cars.
Two outcomes for each trial: defective or not defective, under a defined rule.
The same defect probability for each car: 0.02.
Independence between cars’ defect outcomes.

What could undermine it? A shared production fault might cause several cars to be defective together.
Model input: 2% is the assumed probability in this exercise, not a new estimate from observed factory records.

A binomial distribution need not look normal
A binomial model can be skewed when successes are rare. With only 1.6 defective cars expected per batch, this model places most probability near zero, even though the batch contains 80 cars.
Here, E(X)E(X) is the expected (long-run mean) count and SD(X)SD(X) measures its spread:
E(X)=np=1.6,SD(X)=np(1−p)≈1.252.E(X)=np=1.6,\qquad SD(X)=\sqrt{np(1-p)}\approx1.252.










Most probability is concentrated at a few small counts; there is also a very small tail beyond the displayed counts.
The shape is right-skewed even though n=80n=80.
A normal approximation needs both npnp and n(1−p)n(1-p) to be sufficiently large; “large nn” alone is not enough.
The mean of 1.6 is a long-run average, not a possible count for a single batch.

title: 3.1 Probability Distributions
text:
Poisson: arrivals during a minute
A Poisson distribution models the number of events in a fixed interval. Its parameter λ\lambda is the expected count in that interval; it must match the interval used in the question.
Book example: a bank’s assumed arrival rate during its lunch period is three customers per minute.
Let X=X= number of arrivals in one specified minute.
X∼Poisson⁡(λ=3).X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda=3).

Count events over a defined time or space interval.
State the unit of the rate: three per minute, not three per hour.
A homogeneous Poisson model assumes a suitable constant rate and independent event occurrences.
Groups arriving together or a strong change in the rate may require a different model.

Question: what is the probability of exactly two arrivals? More than two?
Arrival volume alone does not determine queue length or required staffing; service times also matter.

Poisson: exact counts and the complement
The complement rule gives an event’s probability by subtracting the probability of everything outside it from 1. For the bank model with λ=3\lambda=3, “more than two” is the complement of “two or fewer.”
P(X=x)=e−λλxx!.P(X=x)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}.

Exactly two: P(X=2)=0.22404P(X=2)=0.22404, approximately 22.40%.
More than two: P(X>2)=1−P(X≤2)=0.57681P(X>2)=1-P(X\leq2)=0.57681, approximately 57.68%.

dpois(x, lambda) returns P(X=x)P(X=x): exactly x events. pois identifies the Poisson distribution; d gives its probability mass.
ppois(q, lambda) returns P(X≤q)P(X\leq q) by default. p means cumulative probability; lower.tail=FALSE instead returns P(X>q)P(X>q).
lambda=3 is the expected number of arrivals in one minute. The first answer uses count x=2; the second uses cutoff q=2. c() collects and labels the answers.

title: 3.1 Probability Distributions
section: Continuous uniform: probability is interval length
text:
Continuous uniform: probability is interval length
A continuous uniform distribution spreads probability evenly over an interval. The probability of a subinterval equals its length divided by the full interval length; the density is constant throughout.
Assume arrival time TT is uniform from 8 a.m. to noon:
T∼U(8,12),f(t)=112−8=0.25 per hour.T\sim U(8,12),\qquad f(t)=\frac{1}{12-8}=0.25\text{ per hour}.









P(T<9)=9−812−8=0.25.P(T<9)=\frac{9-8}{12-8}=0.25.
Interpretation: the model assigns a 25% chance to arrival before 9 a.m.; this covers one hour of the four-hour window.

Equal-length intervals have equal probabilities.
The mean is (8+12)/2=10(8+12)/2=10 a.m.; 10 a.m. is not a peak.
There is no basis here for saying that 10 a.m. requires especially high staffing.

R function: cumulative uniform probability

punif(q, min, max) returns the probability at or below cutoff q under a continuous uniform model. p means cumulative probability; unif identifies the uniform distribution.
min and max are the model’s lower and upper limits, not values R estimates from data. For arrival time, q=9, min=8 and max=12 are hours.
lower.tail=FALSE requests the probability above q. For diameters, all three values are in millimetres.
For a continuous model, including the cutoff does not change the probability. c() combines two separate answers, both 0.25; the labels identify their contexts.


c(arrival_before_9 = punif(q=9, min=8, max=12),

section: The normal distribution: centre and spread
text:
The normal distribution: centre and spread
The normal distribution is a continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped probability model. Its mean μ\mu locates the centre, and its standard deviation σ\sigma controls the spread.
X∼N(μ,σ2).X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).

A symmetric, bell-shaped model with mean μ\mu and SD σ\sigma.
Mean, median and mode coincide.
The second parameter in this notation is the variance; R’s normal functions ask for the SD.










A normal model has unbounded tails. It may approximate some bounded measurements when impossible tail values are negligible. Salaries, profits and waiting times are not automatically normal.

section: Four R functions: density, probability, cutoff and simulation
text:
Four R functions: density, probability, cutoff and simulation
R provides four related functions for many distributions. The prefix tells us the task; the ending identifies the distribution. For the normal model, the ending is norm.




mean and sd specify the normal model in all four functions. x is a value; q is a cutoff; p is a probability; n is the number of generated values.
All panels use mean 70 and SD 6. The dots show the 12 simulated scores generated below.

Create a small simulated dataset

set.seed(312) makes the random sequence reproducible when this code is rerun in the same R setup. The seed is a chosen starting value, not a sample size.
rnorm(n=12, mean=70, sd=6) generates 12 scores. data.frame(score=...) puts them in a table with one column named score; <- stores that table as simulated_scores. head() displays its first six rows.


set.seed(312)
simulated_scores <- data.frame(score=rnorm(n=12, mean=70, sd=6))
head(simulated_scores)

Read the output: each row is one simulated observation. These are generated values, not collected student records. The model mean is 70 and SD is 6; a sample of 12 will generally have a different mean and SD.
Other distribution families use the same prefixes: binom (binomial), pois (Poisson) and unif (uniform). For discrete models, d gives probability mass.

The empirical rule: approximate normal areas
The empirical rule states that, under a normal model, approximately 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean, respectively.



Interval
Approximate share under a normal model




μ±σ\mu\pm\sigma
68%

95%

99.7%













Use this rule when a roughly normal shape is defensible.
These are rounded model percentages, not guarantees for every sample.
For example, the exact normal area within two SDs is approximately 95.45%.

title: 3.1 Probability Distributions
text:
Worked example: expected exam-score counts
An expected count is the model’s predicted average number in a group: multiply the group size by the probability of the event. We use the rounded empirical-rule percentages here.
A class has 280 students. Assume scores are approximately normal with mean 74 and SD 8.
1. Between 58 and 90
58=74−2(8),90=74+2(8).58=74-2(8),\qquad90=74+2(8).

Both limits are two SDs from the mean.
Approximate count: 280×0.95=266280\times0.95=266 students.

2. Above 90

The upper tail beyond two SDs is approximately (1−0.95)/2=0.025(1-0.95)/2=0.025.
Approximate count: 280×0.025=7280\times0.025=7 students.

Interpretation: these are approximate model-based expected counts. They are not the observed class counts or a guarantee about this class.

text:
z-scores: expressing position in SD units
A z-score tells us how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean. Subtract the mean from the value, then divide by the standard deviation; a positive result is above the mean.
z=x−μσ.z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}.



z-score
Interpretation

At the mean

One SD above the mean


−2
Two SDs below the mean



For the exam example:
z58=58−748=−2,z90=90−748=2.z_{58}=\frac{58-74}{8}=-2,\qquad
z_{90}=\frac{90-74}{8}=2.

Standardisation cancels the measurement units.
You can calculate a standard score without assuming normality.
Converting that score into a standard normal probability requires a normal model.
A z-score rule can flag an observation for investigation; it is not a reason to delete it automatically.

Normal probability: start with the event
Under a normal model, the probability of exceeding a threshold is the area to its right under the density curve. Standardising the threshold lets us find that same area on the standard normal distribution, which has mean 0 and SD 1.
Assume exam score XX is normal with mean 70 and SD 6.
Question: what is the probability of a score above 75?
P(X>75)=P(Z>75−706)=P(Z>0.83333).P(X>75)=P\left(Z>\frac{75-70}{6}\right)
=P(Z>0.83333).

section: The same probability in Excel and R
text:
The same probability in Excel and R
Excel and R calculate normal probabilities directly from a threshold, mean and SD. Both normally return the area below the threshold; to answer “above 75,” request the upper tail or subtract the lower-tail probability from 1.
The question remains score above 75, with mean 70 and SD 6.
Excel
=1-NORM.DIST(75,70,6,TRUE)
R: what the function and arguments mean

pnorm(q, mean, sd) returns the probability at or below cutoff q under a normal model. p means cumulative probability; norm identifies the normal distribution.
q=75 is the score threshold, mean=70 sets the model’s centre and sd=6 sets its standard deviation, not its variance.
lower.tail=FALSE requests P(X>75)P(X>75) instead of P(X≤75)P(X\leq75). <- stores the result in p; c() displays it alongside 100*p, its percentage.


p <- pnorm(q=75, mean=70, sd=6, lower.tail=FALSE)
c(probability=p,percentage=100*p)

probability  percentage 
   0.202328   20.232838 


Interpretation: the model assigns a probability of approximately 0.20233, or 20.233%, to an exam score above 75.

lower.tail=FALSE asks for the area above the threshold.
A probability of 0.20233 is not 0.20233%.
Table rounding explains 20.33% versus the unrounded software result of 20.23%.
For a normal interval, subtract two cumulative probabilities: for example, P(64<X<76)=Φ(1)−Φ(−1)≈0.68269P(64<X<76)=\Phi(1)-\Phi(-1)\approx0.68269.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Variables and atomic data types

A variable is a name that refers to a stored object. <- assigns the value on the right to the name on the left.
R is case sensitive: age and Age are different names.
# starts a comment; R ignores the rest of that line.


age <- 25          # Store a number
name <- "Alice"    # Store text
is_registered <- TRUE
age

[1] 25



The types you will use most
An atomic vector holds values of one underlying type. A single value is a vector of length one.



Type
Example
Meaning




Double
72.5 or 25
Numbers, including decimal values


Integer
25L
Whole numbers stored as integers


Character
"Alice"
Text inside quotation marks


Logical
TRUE, FALSE
Truth values used in conditions



These are the main types needed here. R also supports complex and raw atomic types.


Finding the type

typeof(x) reports the underlying storage type of object x.
class(x) reports the object’s class, which helps determine how R handles it.
str(object) displays a compact overview of an object’s structure.


typeof(age)

[1] "double"

class(age)

[1] "numeric"

typeof(25L)

[1] "integer"

typeof(name)

[1] "character"

typeof(is_registered)

[1] "logical"


For age, typeof() returns "double" and class() returns "numeric". These describe the same object in different ways.


Calling a function
In round(x = 12.345, digits = 2), round is the function, x is the number and digits specifies decimal places. Named arguments make each input’s role explicit.

round(x = 12.345, digits = 2)

[1] 12.35


The result is 12.35. Use ?round in the Console to open the function’s help page.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Vectors sequences and selection

Combining values
c() combines its comma-separated arguments into a vector. length(x) counts the elements of vector x.

ages <- c(20, 22, 25, 28, 30)
length(ages)

[1] 5



The result is 5: five ages are stored.
Atomic vectors have one type. c(20, "Alice") converts the number to text so both elements can be character values.
Arithmetic works element by element: ages + 1 adds one to every age; ages * 2 doubles every age. ^ raises values to a power.



Creating sequences

: makes a sequence in steps of one, upwards or downwards.
seq() allows another step size: from is the start, to is the limit and by is the step.
rep() repeats values: x supplies the value and times gives the number of repetitions.


1:5

[1] 1 2 3 4 5

seq(from = 2, to = 10, by = 2)

[1]  2  4  6  8 10

rep(x = 0, times = 3)

[1] 0 0 0




Selecting elements
Square brackets [] select positions. R starts counting at 1.

ages[3]           # Third value: 25

[1] 25

ages[2:4]         # Positions 2, 3 and 4: 22, 25, 28

[1] 22 25 28

ages[c(1, 5)]     # First and fifth values: 20, 30

[1] 20 30


2:4 creates the position vector; ages[2:4] uses it to select values. The colon itself does not perform selection.


Selecting with a condition
>= means greater than or equal to. The comparison produces one logical result for each age. Inside [], R retains the positions marked TRUE.

ages >= 25

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE

ages[ages >= 25]

[1] 25 28 30


The selected ages are 25, 28 and 30.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Logic decisions and repetition

Comparing values



Operator
Meaning
Operator
Meaning




>
Greater than
<
Less than


>=
At least
<=
At most


==
Equal to
!=
Not equal to


&
Elementwise AND
|
Elementwise OR


!
NOT






Use <- to assign a value and == to compare values.
AND requires both conditions; OR requires at least one; NOT reverses a logical value.
Use full TRUE and FALSE, rather than their reassignable shortcuts T and F.


ages[(ages >= 22) & (ages <= 28)]

[1] 22 25 28


This keeps the ages between 22 and 28 inclusive: 22, 25 and 28.


Conditional branching
if evaluates one condition. When it is TRUE, the first block runs; otherwise the else block runs. Braces {} group instructions. The condition must be a single, nonmissing logical value.

score <- 65
if (score >= 50) {
  print("Pass")
} else {
  print("Below the pass mark")
}

[1] "Pass"


The output is "Pass". Add else if (another_condition) before else when you need a further branch. For two single-value conditions in an if, use && for AND or || for OR.


Repetition with a for loop
for takes each value from a vector in turn. Here, number becomes 1, then 2, then 3. Each time, the block squares it and prints the result.

for (number in 1:3) {
  print(number^2)
}

[1] 1
[1] 4
[1] 9


The results are 1, 4 and 9. For this calculation, (1:3)^2 also works directly on the vector. A loop is useful when each repetition requires several instructions.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Working with a data frame
A data frame is a table: rows contain observations and columns contain variables. Columns can have different types, but they must have the same number of rows.

A small example
data.frame() combines named columns into a table. Here, each row represents one person; the values are illustrative.

people <- data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Eva"),
  age = c(25, 30, 22)
)
people

   name age
1 Alice  25
2   Bob  30
3   Eva  22



people$age extracts the age column as a vector.
people[1:2, ] selects the first two rows. A blank column position means all columns.
str(people) reports the column names, types and example values.



Reading the supplied CSV
read.csv() imports a comma-separated file. Its file argument gives the path relative to the course project root. head(x, n = 3) displays only the first three rows of x.

superstore <- read.csv(file = "data/r-introduction/superstore.csv")
head(x = superstore[c("Category", "Sales", "Profit")], n = 3)

   Category  Sales   Profit
1 Furniture 261.96  41.9136
2 Furniture 731.94 219.5820
3 Furniture 731.94 219.5820



This is the original fictitious Superstore tutorial data with 2014–2017 order dates, separate from the 2023–2025 practical data.
Each row is an order line, not necessarily a distinct order or customer.
read.csv() makes names containing spaces syntactically valid; for example, Order ID becomes Order.ID. The three names used here are unchanged.



Missing values

NA represents a missing value. Test it with is.na(x), not x == NA.
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) calculates the arithmetic mean after omitting missing values. Omitting values changes which observations enter the calculation.


values <- c(10, NA, 20)
is.na(values)

[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE

mean(x = values, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 15


The missingness check returns FALSE TRUE FALSE; the mean of the two observed values is 15.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Preparing data with dplyr
dplyr supplies functions for selecting, filtering, sorting, transforming and summarising tables.

Install once and load each session
install.packages() downloads packages named in its pkgs argument. Run this cell once in an internet-connected session. Installation is excluded when rendering this document.

install.packages(pkgs = c("dplyr", "ggplot2"))

library() makes an installed package available in the current session.

library(dplyr)



Select filter sort and calculate
Each function below receives a table first. Subsequent arguments name columns, supply a condition or define a calculation.

select() keeps columns; filter() keeps rows satisfying its condition.
arrange() sorts rows. desc() requests descending order.
mutate() adds or changes a column. Here, the new column expresses each line’s sales after an illustrative 10 percent increase; it is not an observed value.


sales_columns <- select(superstore, Category, Sales, Profit)
technology <- filter(sales_columns, Category == "Technology")
largest_first <- arrange(technology, desc(Sales))
sales_example <- mutate(largest_first, Sales_plus_10pct = Sales * 1.10)



Group and summarise

%>% passes the result on its left into the first argument of the next function. Read it as “then”. It becomes available when dplyr is loaded.
group_by(Category) forms a group for each category.
summarise() returns one summary row per group here. n() counts order lines; sum(Sales) totals their sales. .groups = "drop" removes grouping from the result.


category_totals <- superstore %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  summarise(lines = n(), total_sales = sum(Sales), .groups = "drop")
category_totals

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Category        lines total_sales
  <chr>           <int>       <dbl>
1 Furniture        2122     742732.
2 Office Supplies  6027     719062.
3 Technology       1847     836154.


Each row reports a category’s line count and sales total, not its distinct order count. These calculations assume the relevant values are observed; investigate missing data before summarising a new file.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Conventional plots in base R
Base R includes plotting functions without an additional package. Choose a plot to match the variable and question.

Histogram of a numerical variable
hist() groups numerical values into intervals and plots their frequencies. x supplies the observations; breaks suggests a number of intervals; main sets the title and xlab labels the horizontal axis. Actual interval boundaries can differ from the suggested count.

hist(x = superstore$Quantity, breaks = 10,
     main = "Quantity per order line", xlab = "Quantity", col = "gray75")








col controls the fill colour. Read the horizontal axis as quantity and the vertical axis as the number of order lines in each interval. Quantity is a discrete numerical variable.


Bar plot of category counts
table() counts observations in each category. barplot() uses those counts as bar heights; height supplies the counts, and ylab labels the vertical axis.

category_counts <- table(superstore$Category)
barplot(height = category_counts, main = "Order lines by category",
        ylab = "Number of order lines", col = "gray75")








Compare the separate bars to compare categories. A bar chart represents categories; a histogram represents numerical intervals.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Boxplots and scatter plots

Boxplot of a numerical variable
boxplot() summarises a distribution. x supplies the values and ylab labels the numerical axis.

boxplot(x = superstore$Sales, main = "Sales per order line",
        ylab = "Sales in US dollars", col = "gray75")









The line inside the box is the median; the box spans the middle half of the observations.
Default whiskers reach the most extreme observations within 1.5 box lengths of the box edges. Values beyond them appear separately.
Separate points indicate potentially unusual values, not proven errors. Large sales values stretch this plot’s scale.



Scatter plot of two numerical variables
plot(x, y) places each order line at its sales value horizontally and profit value vertically. pch = 16 selects filled circles; cex = 0.4 reduces their size.

plot(x = superstore$Sales, y = superstore$Profit,
     main = "Sales and profit by order line",
     xlab = "Sales in US dollars", ylab = "Profit in US dollars",
     pch = 16, cex = 0.4, col = "gray45")








Look for patterns, negative profits and unusual lines. Points may overlap. An association in these fictitious observational records does not establish a causal relationship.

title: Introduction to R
text:
A brief introduction to ggplot2
ggplot2 builds a plot by combining data, mappings and drawing layers. We use the same sales and profit columns as in the base R scatter plot.

library(ggplot2)

Before running the next cell:

ggplot(data = superstore) supplies the table.
mapping = aes(x = Sales, y = Profit) maps columns to the horizontal and vertical axes. aes() describes how data control visual positions or appearance.
+ adds a layer to a ggplot. geom_point() draws one point per row; size controls point size and colour sets one fixed colour.
labs() supplies the title and axis labels. theme_minimal() simplifies the background.


ggplot(data = superstore, mapping = aes(x = Sales, y = Profit)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, colour = "gray45") +
  labs(title = "Sales and profit by order line",
       x = "Sales in US dollars", y = "Profit in US dollars") +
  theme_minimal()








Read this plot in the same way as the base R scatter plot. The main new idea is assembling a graph from layers.

Combining dplyr and ggplot2

First prepare the table with dplyr, then pass it into ggplot() using %>%.
The pipe supplies the table as ggplot’s first argument, data. You can therefore omit data = ... in the piped call.
Use %>% to pass a table between functions; use + to add layers after ggplot() has created the plot.
The next two examples use this same workflow: prepare data, map variables, draw the plot, add labels.

title: Introduction to R
section: Filter data then draw a histogram
text:
Filter data then draw a histogram
Question: How does quantity per order line vary within Technology?

filter(Category == "Technology") keeps only Technology lines. The incoming table is supplied by %>%.
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = Quantity)) receives that filtered table and maps Quantity to the horizontal axis.
geom_histogram() counts observations within numerical intervals. binwidth = 1 sets intervals one unit wide; boundary = 0.5 places their edges at half units so each integer quantity has its own interval.
fill sets one fixed bar colour; colour sets the bar outlines. These settings sit outside aes() because they do not depend on a variable.


superstore %>%
  filter(Category == "Technology") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = Quantity)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5,
                 fill = "gray75", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Quantity on Technology order lines",
       x = "Quantity", y = "Number of order lines") +
  theme_minimal()









Each bar counts Technology order lines with that quantity; it does not count distinct orders.
The original superstore table is unchanged: the pipeline passes its filtered result directly to the plot.
labs() and theme_minimal() work just as in the earlier scatter plot. The change is in the data preparation and drawing layer.


Read the pipeline aloud
“Take Superstore, keep Technology lines, use Quantity on the horizontal axis, draw a histogram, then add labels and a simple theme.”

title: Introduction to R
section: Summarise data then draw a bar chart
text:
Summarise data then draw a bar chart
Question: What is the total sales value for each product category?

group_by(Category) and summarise() produce one row per category. sum(Sales) / 1000 expresses each total in thousands of US dollars, stored in the new column sales_thousands.
The next pipe sends this summary table to ggplot(). Map Category to x and sales_thousands to y.
geom_col() uses the supplied y values as bar heights. In contrast, geom_bar() counts rows by default; on this three-row summary table, that would count one row per category instead of showing sales totals.


superstore %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  summarise(sales_thousands = sum(Sales) / 1000, .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = Category, y = sales_thousands)) +
  geom_col(fill = "gray65") +
  labs(title = "Total sales by category",
       x = "Product category", y = "Sales in US$ thousands") +
  theme_minimal()








The bars show sales totals across all tutorial order lines in each category; a height of 800 means US$800,000. This differs from the earlier bar plot of category line counts. fill sets the same grey for every bar.

Check your understanding

Create a numeric vector with c(). Check its type and select positions 2 to 4.
Use a logical condition to keep values above a threshold. Write an if and else for one value.
Write a for loop that prints the squares of 1 to 5.
Filter Superstore to Furniture lines and calculate their total sales.
Draw a histogram of Profit. Explain what one bar represents.
Adapt the piped histogram to Furniture lines. Keep the quantity intervals unchanged.
Adapt the grouped bar chart to total Profit by Category. Update the title and vertical-axis label.

Hypothetical commercial assumptions

Contribution margin per additional case: $4, $6 or $8.
Opportunity cost of the display: $80 per store per week.
These are assignment assumptions, not COLA observations or textbook financial data.
Assume the measured sales difference represents incremental cases and the chosen margin applies to them; discuss why this may fail.

# For each assumed margin, calculate:

Multiplying the sales interval by a fixed positive margin gives a conditional interval under that assumed margin.
It does not include uncertainty in costs, margins, cannibalization or future display effects.
Treat a zero-crossing interval as uncertainty about the assumed commercial threshold, not proof of no value.
